# Apple Computer,   Chapter One 1989

**Source**: /Volumes/NvME-Satechi/steve-jobs.ai/Database_Steve_Jobs/1980s/Apple Computer,   Chapter One 1989.mp4

**Transcribed**: 2025-12-31 10:02

---

**[Narrator]**: In 1923, Lon Chaney's brilliant characterization of Quasimodo in the Hunchback of Notre Dame played on the audience's tendency to stereotype, to prejudge individuals according to their appearance, rather than understand them for who they really were.

**[Narrator]**: It's been nearly a century since the Hunchback of Notre Dame horrified audiences in the silent movie houses. But have attitudes changed much in 95 years? Or do we still judge far too quickly the content by the cover?

**[Narrator]**: Oh, where do we go from here?

**[Computer Voice]**: Show me writer's block. The current project is untitled. To continue, you may wish to review your outline, explore the suggestion box, or view great writers' methods. Sometimes a short break helps to stimulate ideas. Perhaps you'd enjoy a pleasant walk.

**[Narrator]**: Oh, it's not that bad yet. Um, show me the outline.

**[Computer Voice]**: Your next heading is Technology's impact on attitudes toward people with disabilities. The subheading is the catalyst for change.

**[Narrator]**: Okay, I need some examples. Um, where can we go for information about how attitudes and expectations have changed toward people with disability in the last, say, 15 or 20 years?

**[Computer Voice]**: I have a list of consultants who provide data excerpts in related areas. There is also a media index called Capabilities Enhancement.

**[Narrator]**: Good, show me the index, hold the list.

**[Child 1]**: Did you guys just finish an entire box of cookies?

**[Child 2]**: Mom, the science said makes you hungry. Besides, it wasn't entire box. You had some too.

**[Narrator]**: One, I had one. Well, maybe two. Honey, it's too early for dinner. I'm working against a deadline. Can you wait about an hour?

**[Child 2]**: Maybe.

**[Narrator]**: The lonely, unappreciated scientific genius forges on, despite enormous odds.

**[Narrator]**: Right. Happy forging. Bye.

**[Scientist]**: Okay, so much for the hydrogen iodide. One more unit and we're done. Now, wait a second. What did they think would happen if we used chlorine with this? Zach, don't do this to me, please. Come on, one last sense of adventure. Frustrate me.

**[Narrator]**: Show me this one.

**[Man]**: Hi, Cindy.

**[Computer Voice]**: Well, hi there, Cindy. What's cooking today?

**[Cindy]**: I'm cooking some strawberry cake for Mom's birthday.

**[Computer Voice]**: A strawberry cake for Mom's birthday? Okay. First, let's get our equipment. A big spoon, a mixing bowl, and your special measuring cup.

**[Cindy]**: Okay.

**[Computer Voice]**: The first thing to do is to put the measuring cup on the scale.

**[Computer Voice]**: Good. Now, pour in three-quarters cup of milk.

**[Computer Voice]**: That's it. Keep pouring.

**[Computer Voice]**: Cindy, you stopped. You need one-quarter cup more. Here, I'll show you. Fill it up to the yellow line.

**[Cindy]**: Okay, because of the crack.

**[Computer Voice]**: That's it. Keep pouring. All the way up to the yellow line.

**[Cindy]**: That's it.

**[Computer Voice]**: Good. Now, make sure you stir the batter until it is smooth and creamy.

**[Computer Voice]**: Cindy, are you finished yet?

**[Cindy]**: Yep.

**[Computer Voice]**: Did you get all of the lumps out?

**[Cindy]**: Mhm.

**[Computer Voice]**: Okay. Now, put the baking bowl into the microwave and I'll take care of the rest. I'll call you when it's ready, then we can put on the strawberries.

**[Cindy]**: [Laughter]

**[Computer Voice]**: Well, Cindy, that should just about do it. I hope you had fun making Mom's birthday cake. I think she'll really be surprised.

**[Narrator]**: Good. Save this in the presentation folder. Show me the main index again.

**[Scientist 1]**: It's not doing anything.

**[Scientist 2]**: Good. We'll just submit the results and move to the next one.

**[Scientist 1]**: No, wait, maybe we should try heating it up.

**[Scientist 2]**: I can't believe this.

**[Narrator]**: Show me this one.

**[Woman]**: Sorry, I said, if you'll let my advertising deficit ride through this quarter, I promise to make it up to you in the fall.

**[Man]**: Steph, that's what you said last year.

**[Woman]**: I know, but this year I'm planning a huge promotion to get ready for the holidays. I think we can at least double our normal business for the season. How much stock would you need?

**[Man]**: I'm estimating about 10,000 pieces. And I want to run four weeks of full-page ads in the mailer.

**[Man]**: Four weeks, really?

**[Man]**: I think we can work something out.

**[Man]**: Well, I'll have to talk with my sales manager, but yes, I think we can.

**[Waiter]**: Bonjour, Madame. Bonjour, Monsieur.

**[Woman]**: Bonjour, Pierre. Nice to be back.

**[Waiter]**: Monsieur, vous désirez un apéritif?

**[Woman]**: Non, merci. Thanks. Would you like a drink?

**[Man]**: No, no, thank you.

**[Woman]**: I think we'll just see the menu, thank you.

**[Waiter]**: Très bien, Madame. Tout de suite.

**[Man]**: Impressive. I didn't know you spoke French.

**[Woman]**: Well, I don't really, but I understand a little.

**[Scientist 1]**: Wow, I think we just discovered hydrochloric acid, partner. Now let's add the fluorine.

**[Scientist 2]**: Zach, I just realized something. And now for the hydrogen. Zach, don't these halogens, as you go up the periodic table, don't they get smaller too?

**[Scientist 1]**: You were saying?

**[Scientist 2]**: Never mind.

**[Professor]**: Gentlemen, we can discuss this particular reaction tomorrow in lab. In the meantime, please review the program on halogens before it means the end of civilization as we know it.

**[Scientist 1]**: I'll review it right away, sir. Good luck.

**[Scientist 2]**: Some partner.

**[Narrator]**: As we move into the 20s, we begin an era of discovery where doing even simple things can bring great power. Each new year brings the hope that even our bravest dreams may yet come true. Quasimodo is a symbol of the last century's sometimes backward ways. Then people like Stephanie and Cindy are symbols of the future. Technology is not the only answer, but it can be and is a catalyst for change.

**[Narrator]**: Stop. Let's shut down.

**[Computer Voice]**: This document is unnamed. What is your title?

**[Narrator]**: Good question.

**[Narrator]**: Hey Einstein, you got any good ideas what I should call this thing?

**[Child]**: Call what?

**[Narrator]**: The project I'm working on.

**[Child]**: I don't know. Is it finished?

**[Narrator]**: No, I just got started really.

**[Narrator]**: Chapter One, that's not a bad idea. Okay, you guys, let's see.
